title: Entrepreneurship
summary: An entrepreneur is a person who identifies a business opportunity, turns the idea into action, collects resources, sets up and manages a new enterprise and bears its risk. Entrepreneurship is the process of initiating, creating and managing such an enterprise — a creative, risk-bearing activity. Entrepreneurs are moderate (calculated) risk-takers, not gamblers; they are made by training and experience, not only born; they do things differently from others and constantly strive for excellence; and they generate employment for others.

(1) Provides employment — to the entrepreneur and to others, so it reduces unemployment. (2) Contributes to research and development — most innovations come from entrepreneurs. (3) Creates wealth for individuals and the nation, adding goods and services to the economy. (4) Promotes balanced regional development by setting up units in small towns and villages. (5) Raises the standard of living and increases exports. Small enterprises contribute to national development through employment, use of local resources and skills, a large share of production and exports, equitable distribution of income and support to large industries as suppliers.

(1) Initiative — a man of action who seizes opportunities. (2) Willingness to assume risk. (3) Ability to learn from experience — not repeating mistakes. (4) Motivation — the urge to complete what is started, which keeps a small business going through difficulties and inspires employees. (5) Self-confidence. (6) Decision-making ability — right decisions at the right time, so opportunities are not missed and losses are avoided. Also hard work, creativity, alertness and foresight, leadership, and taking responsibility for one's actions. Success depends on both hard work and a good idea. Lack of confidence is not a quality.

(1) Identifying entrepreneurial opportunities — the first function; sensing human needs (food, fashion, education) faster than others. (2) Turning ideas into action — collecting information and setting goals. (3) Feasibility study — assessing market demand, inputs, costs and problems, prepared as a business plan or project report. (4) Resourcing — arranging money, machines, materials and men. (5) Setting up the enterprise — legal formalities, location, premises, machinery. (6) Managing the enterprise — production, men, finance and marketing. (7) Growth and development — setting higher goals. Innovation and risk bearing run through all of these.

Anyone can start a small business — rich or not, educated or not, rural or urban. Factors to consider: (1) arrangement of finance — fixed capital for land, building, machinery and furniture, and working capital for raw materials, wages, rent and bills; sources: own savings, friends and relatives, banks and financial institutions, government schemes (MUDRA, SIDBI); (2) selection of the line of business according to market demand, profitability and risk; (3) choice of the form of organisation — usually sole proprietorship or partnership; (4) location — near raw materials, the market, labour, transport and banking; a retail shop near residential areas; (5) availability of skilled and semi-skilled labour; (6) technology and machinery, sources of raw material, marketing (sales promotion) and legal formalities. A small business needs only a small amount of working capital.

vsa: Explain briefly feasibility study and identifying entrepreneurial opportunities as functions of an entrepreneur.

Identifying opportunities: sensing changing human needs (food, fashion, education) faster than others and finding a business in them — the first function.
Feasibility study: studying whether the proposed product will succeed — market demand, inputs, costs, sources and problems — and preparing a business plan or project report.
Write a short note on entrepreneurship.

Entrepreneurship is the process of identifying an opportunity, turning the idea into an enterprise, arranging resources, managing it and bearing its risk. It creates employment and wealth, encourages innovation and helps the development of the nation.
State two points of importance of entrepreneurship.

(1) It provides employment to the entrepreneur and others and reduces unemployment.
(2) It creates wealth and new products, contributing to research and national development.
sa: How would motivation help an entrepreneur in running a small business?

(1) It gives him the drive to keep working until the goal is reached, even in difficulties.
(2) It keeps him enthusiastic about improving products and service.
(3) A motivated owner inspires his employees, which raises their output and loyalty.
How can small enterprises contribute to national development?

(1) They provide employment to a large number of people with little capital.
(2) They use local resources and skills and promote balanced regional development.
(3) They add to production and exports and lead to a fairer distribution of income.

or: Why is decision-making ability important for an entrepreneur?

An entrepreneur must take many decisions — what to produce, where, how much, at what price. Right and timely decisions help him seize opportunities before others, avoid losses and keep the business growing; delay can mean a missed opportunity and loss.

sa: What are the sources of finance for setting up a small business?

(1) Own savings (self-contribution).
(2) Loans from friends and relatives.
(3) Loans from banks and financial institutions, and government schemes such as MUDRA and SIDBI.
State any three qualities of a successful entrepreneur.

(1) Initiative — taking prompt action on opportunities.
(2) Willingness to take risk.
(3) Self-confidence and decision-making ability.

or: What factors would you consider if you start a small enterprise to produce paper cups?

(1) Finance — fixed capital for machines and working capital for paper and wages.
(2) Location — near suppliers of paper and near the market (hotels, tea stalls), with power and transport.
(3) Availability of labour, technology and machinery; demand in the market; legal formalities.

sa: Describe any four qualities of a successful entrepreneur.
(1) Initiative. (2) Willingness to assume risk. (3) Ability to learn from experience. (4) Motivation. (Also self-confidence and decision-making ability.)
la: What is entrepreneurship? Explain any four functions of an entrepreneur.

Entrepreneurship is the process of identifying a business opportunity and creating and managing an enterprise to exploit it, bearing the risk involved.
(1) Identifying opportunities — spotting unmet needs in the market.
(2) Feasibility study — studying demand, costs and inputs and preparing a business plan.
(3) Resourcing — arranging finance, machines, materials and people.
(4) Setting up and managing the enterprise — legal formalities, location, production, finance and marketing.
(5) Growth and development — setting higher goals and striving for excellence.

or: What factors would you consider if you start a small enterprise to produce bathing soap?

(1) Finance — fixed capital (machines, premises) and working capital (oils, chemicals, wages).
(2) Line of business — demand for soap, competition, profitability.
(3) Form of organisation — sole proprietorship or partnership.
(4) Location — near raw-material suppliers and the market, with transport, water and power.
(5) Labour, technology, legal formalities (licences, quality marks) and marketing.

(2) Selection of the line of business — demand, profitability and risk.
(3) Choice of form of organisation — sole proprietorship or partnership.
(4) Location — raw material, market, labour, transport and banking.
(5) Availability of labour and technology; legal formalities and marketing.
